lessons.title: subtle
lessons.meaning: Not obvious; requiring attention to notice.
lessons.example: There is a subtle difference in tone between those replies.
lessons.notes: Use subtle for a difference or effect that is hard to notice, not one that is unimportant. Subtly is the adverb: Her tone changed subtly.
lessons.conversation:
A: Do those replies sound the same to you?
B: There is a subtle difference in tone.
A: What do you notice?
B: The second sounds slightly warmer, though the wording barely changes.
lessons.exercise: Describe a subtle difference between two messages and explain its effect. Model: Adding “when you have time” makes the request subtly less urgent.

lessons.title: discrepancy
lessons.meaning: A difference between things that should match.
lessons.example: We found a discrepancy between the invoice and the payment.
lessons.notes: Use a discrepancy between two figures or records that should agree. The word identifies a mismatch without assuming dishonesty.
lessons.conversation:
A: Does the invoice match the payment?
B: No. There is a discrepancy of twenty dollars.
A: Could that be a delivery charge?
B: Possibly. Let us check before calling it an error.
lessons.exercise: Describe two records that disagree without assigning blame. Model: There is a discrepancy between the invoice total and the amount received.

lessons.title: phase out
lessons.example: The company is phasing out the old system.
lessons.notes: Phase out means remove gradually, not stop overnight. It is separable: phase the system out; phase it out. Use phasing for an ongoing transition.
lessons.conversation:
A: Are we stopping the old system immediately?
B: No. We are phasing it out over three months.
A: Will both systems run during the transition?
B: Yes, until everyone has moved to the new one.
lessons.exercise: Describe a gradual transition using phase out and a time frame. Model: We will phase out paper forms over the next six months.

lessons.title: fall through
lessons.example: Our travel plans fell through at the last minute.
lessons.notes: Fall through is intransitive: the deal fell through, not we fell the deal through. It describes an arrangement that fails to happen; say fell through for the past.
lessons.conversation:
A: Are you still taking the weekend trip?
B: No. Our plans fell through when the booking was canceled.
A: Could you rearrange it for next month?
B: Yes. We will check dates before making new plans.
lessons.exercise: Explain why an arrangement fell through. Model: The agreement fell through because the two sides could not agree on a price.

lessons.title: up in the air
lessons.example: Our weekend plans are still up in the air.
lessons.notes: Use still up in the air for an undecided outcome or arrangement. It does not mean something has definitely been canceled.
lessons.conversation:
A: Have you decided where to go this weekend?
B: Our plans are still up in the air.
A: What are you waiting for?
B: The weather forecast. Then we can choose.
lessons.exercise: Name an undecided plan and what would settle it. Model: The venue is up in the air until we know how many guests are coming.

lessons.title: a learning curve
lessons.meaning: The process or difficulty of gaining new skills.
lessons.example: The new software has a steep learning curve.
lessons.notes: A steep learning curve commonly means a task is difficult to learn quickly in everyday speech. Learning curve refers to learning over time, not a literal physical curve.
lessons.conversation:
A: Is the new software easy to learn?
B: It has a steep learning curve at first.
A: What makes it challenging?
B: The unfamiliar shortcuts, though practice is making them easier.
lessons.exercise: Describe what makes a new skill difficult at first. Model: The editing software has a steep learning curve because its controls are unfamiliar.

lessons.title: I do not want to overstep.
lessons.meaning: Show awareness of another person’s boundaries or authority.
lessons.example: I do not want to overstep, but may I offer a suggestion?
lessons.notes: Overstep means exceed a boundary or your authority. This softening phrase should precede a respectful request, not excuse intrusive advice.
lessons.conversation:
A: I do not want to overstep, but may I suggest a different approach?
B: Of course. What did you have in mind?
A: Could we ask the team before changing their schedule?
B: That sounds reasonable. Let us check with them first.
lessons.exercise: Offer a suggestion while respecting a boundary. Model: I do not want to overstep, but would you like another perspective on the draft?

lessons.title: Wish about the past
lessons.meaning: Use wish + past perfect to express regret about the past.
lessons.example: I wish I had asked more questions.
lessons.notes: For regret about a completed past event, use wish + had + past participle. I wish I had asked means I did not ask; it cannot change the past.
lessons.conversation:
A: Did you ask about the deadline?
B: No. I wish I had asked more questions.
A: What would you do differently next time?
B: Prepare a list beforehand so I do not forget.
lessons.exercise: Express regret: You did not save the file. Model: I wish I had saved the file before closing the program.

lessons.title: What is keeping you busy these days?
lessons.meaning: Invite a broad answer about work, hobbies, or family.
lessons.example: What is keeping you busy these days?
lessons.notes: These days asks about a current period, not only today. Let the person choose work, hobbies or family; follow up on the detail they offer.
lessons.conversation:
A: What is keeping you busy these days?
B: I am learning to bake bread.
A: What got you interested in it?
B: A friend showed me how to make a simple loaf.
A: Have you tried anything more challenging?
B: Sourdough, though I am still getting the timing right.
A: That sounds rewarding. What do you enjoy most?
B: Sharing a fresh loaf with people. What have you been up to?
lessons.exercise: Answer the opening with an activity and a detail, then ask a question back. Model: I am learning to bake bread on weekends. What is keeping you busy?

lessons.title: Confidence grows when practice becomes a habit.
lessons.meaning: Regular repetition builds ease over time.
lessons.example: Before her daily speaking practice, Maya reminded herself, “Confidence grows when practice becomes a habit.”
lessons.notes: Use this reflection to encourage consistent practice. Becomes a habit means an action grows familiar through repetition; avoid presenting confidence as an immediate result.
lessons.conversation:
A: I still feel nervous speaking English.
B: “Confidence grows when practice becomes a habit.” Try five minutes daily.
A: So I should focus on consistency, not perfection?
B: Exactly. Start with something you can repeat.
lessons.exercise: Use the quote to encourage a friend, then suggest one realistic practice habit. Model: Read a short paragraph aloud every morning.
